title: Linear Algebra for Quantum Mechanics
intro: Every calculation in quantum mechanics is a matrix calculation over the complex numbers. This page collects the pieces used on every later page: inner products, adjoints, Hermitian and unitary matrices, eigen-decomposition, matrix exponentials and Kronecker products.

blocks.text: Complex vectors and the inner product

A state of a $d$-level system is a column vector $v \in \mathbb{C}^d$. The inner product conjugates the first argument, $\langle u, v\rangle = \sum_i \bar u_i v_i$, so that $\langle v, v\rangle = \sum_i \vert v_i\vert^2$ is real and non-negative: it is the squared length. Two vectors are orthogonal when their inner product is zero, and an orthonormal basis is $d$ mutually orthogonal unit vectors.
Numpy's `np.vdot(u, v)` conjugates its first argument and computes exactly this; `u @ v` does not conjugate and is the wrong tool for complex states.
The adjoint, Hermitian and unitary matrices
The adjoint (conjugate transpose) of a matrix is $A^\dagger = \bar A^{\top}$. It is defined so that $\langle u, Av\rangle = \langle A^\dagger u, v\rangle$. Two families of matrices matter most.

items: Hermitian: $A^\dagger = A$. Their eigenvalues are real and eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are orthogonal. Observables and Hamiltonians are Hermitian.
Unitary: $U^\dagger U = I$. They preserve inner products, hence lengths and angles, and their eigenvalues have modulus 1. Time evolution and quantum gates are unitary.

blocks.text: Eigen-decomposition (the spectral theorem)
Every Hermitian matrix can be written in terms of its eigenvalues $\lambda_k$ and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors $v_k$:

blocks.caption: The spectral theorem: V is unitary, with the eigenvectors as its columns.

blocks.text: This is the most useful identity on the shelf. It says a Hermitian matrix just stretches space by real factors along a set of perpendicular directions. Each $v_kv_k^\dagger$ is the projector onto one direction, which is how measurement outcomes will be defined.
Functions of matrices and the exponential

Because of the decomposition, any function of a Hermitian matrix is defined by applying the function to the eigenvalues: $f(A) = V\,\mathrm{diag}(f(\lambda))\,V^\dagger$. The one that matters is the exponential:

blocks.caption: For Hermitian A this is unitary: each eigenvalue becomes a phase.

blocks.text: This is how every QRC simulator on this site builds its time-evolution operator: diagonalise the Hamiltonian once with `np.linalg.eigh`, then reuse the eigenbasis for any time. The power series $e^{X} = \sum_n X^n/n!$ gives the same result and is what `scipy.linalg.expm` computes for general matrices. Note that $e^{A+B} = e^Ae^B$ only when $AB = BA$; the gap between the two is what Trotterisation (#/quantum/qubits/gates-and-circuits) controls.
The commutator

The commutator $[A, B] = AB - BA$ measures how far two matrices are from commuting. Commuting Hermitian matrices share an eigenbasis, so they can be measured together and their exponentials can be split. Non-commuting ones cannot, and that single fact is behind the uncertainty principle, the order-dependence of rotations, and Trotter error.
Kronecker (tensor) products

For an $m\times m$ matrix $A$ and an $n\times n$ matrix $B$, the Kronecker product $A\otimes B$ is the $mn\times mn$ block matrix whose $(i,j)$ block is $A_{ij}B$. It is how state spaces and operators of separate systems combine (Composite Systems (#/quantum/many-body/composite-systems)). Two rules carry most of the weight: $(A\otimes B)(C\otimes D) = AC\otimes BD$, and $(A\otimes B)^\dagger = A^\dagger\otimes B^\dagger$. Dimensions multiply, which is why $n$ qubits need $2^n$ amplitudes.
Checking it all numerically

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm
# A random Hermitian matrix, its eigen-decomposition, and the unitary it generates.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = rng.normal(size=(4, 4)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=(4, 4))
H = (A + A.conj().T) / 2                       # Hermitian: H = H^dagger
E, V = np.linalg.eigh(H)                       # real eigenvalues, orthonormal eigenvectors
print("eigenvalues (real):", np.round(E, 3))
print("V unitary:", np.allclose(V.conj().T @ V, np.eye(4)))
print("H = V diag(E) V^dagger:", np.allclose(H, V @ np.diag(E) @ V.conj().T))
U = expm(-1j * H * 0.7)                        # exponential of -i H t
U2 = V @ np.diag(np.exp(-1j * E * 0.7)) @ V.conj().T
print("expm agrees with the eigenbasis formula:", np.allclose(U, U2))
print("U unitary:", np.allclose(U.conj().T @ U, np.eye(4)))
# Kronecker products: dimensions multiply, and (A x B)(C x D) = AC x BD
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]); Z = np.diag([1, -1])
print("X (x) Z is", np.kron(X, Z).shape, "and (X(x)Z)(Z(x)X) = XZ (x) ZX:",
      np.allclose(np.kron(X, Z) @ np.kron(Z, X), np.kron(X @ Z, Z @ X)))

blocks.text: Output of the run: the eigenvalues come out real (−1.891, −0.808, 0.46, 1.371), the eigenvector matrix is unitary, the decomposition rebuilds $H$, `expm` and the eigenbasis formula give the same unitary, and the Kronecker mixed-product rule holds.
Where QRC uses this

items: Every reservoir step $\rho\mapsto U\rho U^\dagger$ uses a unitary built by eigen-decomposition: The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir).
The Liouvillian of Lindblad Dynamics (#/qrc/open-systems/lindblad-dynamics) is built entirely from Kronecker products.
Ridge regression on the readout is real linear algebra: the SVD form on Echo State Networks (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-networks) is the real-valued cousin of the spectral theorem.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: Hermitian or not
blocks.text: Is the matrix with rows $(1, i)$ and $(-i, 2)$ Hermitian? Find its eigenvalues.
solution: The adjoint swaps and conjugates the off-diagonal entries: the top-right entry of $A^\dagger$ is $\overline{-i} = i$, the bottom-left is $\overline{i} = -i$. So $A^\dagger = A$: it is Hermitian.
$\lambda = (3\pm\sqrt5)/2 \approx 2.618$ and $0.382$: real, as they must be.

blocks.title: Exponential of a diagonal matrix
blocks.text: Write $e^{-i\theta Z}$ as a matrix, where $Z$ is diagonal with entries $1$ and $-1$. Is it unitary?
solution: $Z$ is already diagonal, so exponentiate the diagonal: $e^{-i\theta Z} = \mathrm{diag}(e^{-i\theta}, e^{i\theta})$.
Each entry has modulus 1 and the matrix is diagonal, so $U^\dagger U = \mathrm{diag}(1, 1) = I$: unitary.

blocks.title: Sizes of tensor products
blocks.text: A system of one qubit and one 4-level system is described by vectors of what dimension? What is the size of $X\otimes B$ for $X$ a $2\times2$ and $B$ a $4\times4$ matrix?
solution: $X\otimes B$ is $8\times8$, made of four $4\times4$ blocks $X_{ij}B$.
